D.t: Charles Booker trails by 14.8 and wins 2% of simulations. Closing it takes about 122,857 voters switching sides, or 245,713 more net votes from new turnout.
In 8 of 10 simulations the result lands between R +23.3 and R +6.0. Only an unusual polling error changes the winner.

The biggest vote banks for Democrats: Jefferson, a projected net 116,867 votes; Fayette, a projected net 45,587 votes; Franklin, a projected net 3,792 votes. Every point of extra turnout here is worth more than persuasion anywhere else.
The large counties within 12 points: Kenton, R +8.0, 3.7% of the vote; Campbell, R +5.1, 2.2% of the vote; Oldham, R +11.8, 1.8% of the vote; Henderson, R +11.7, 0.9% of the vote.

D.h: Where you run behind the 2024 map
D.t: Against the 2024 presidential vote, Charles Booker runs furthest behind in Laurel, Pulaski, Boone. That is where the forecast sees voters who backed your side two years ago and have not come back yet.

Groups big enough to move the race: White voters, 90% of voters, 40 to 60, where a 5 point gain is worth 4.52 points; Voters who cast ballots in 2022 and 2024, 69% of voters, 42 to 58, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.44 points; Voters without a degree, 67% of voters, 40 to 60, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.35 points.

The forecast's worst groups for Charles Booker: Immigration voters 16 to 84, Small counties 30 to 70, Voters who can afford daily costs 39 to 61. Cutting the loss here is often cheaper than winning new groups.
$310K cash against $2.3M. Outspent: lean on earned media, digital, field and the outside groups, and pick the two or three media markets that decide it.
Registered Democrats cast 56% of the 49,502 ballots in Kentucky so far, against 44% for the other party. That is 3.3 points worse for Democrats than the forecast expected by now.

D.h: What the ballots so far say
D.t: The early vote has moved this forecast 1.2 points away from Charles Booker. Election Day has to make it up: the remaining vote must break harder your way than the forecast expects.
